clue.text: Magnificent pals ate it all, except the last scraps

indicators.note: each of the four words is to be read without its final scrap, the last letter dropped from every one

explanation.surface: A greedy friend eats everything on the plate, leaving only a few scraps.
explanation.walkthrough: Dropping the last letter of each of 'pals ate it all' (S, E, T, L) leaves PAL AT I AL.
explanation.definitionFit: Something fit for a palace is grand, which is a synonym for magnificent.

clue.text: Short request to play Scotsman's part is common

indicators.note: short tells us to cut the last letter off the word for request

parts.note: a plea is a request
to play a part is to be someone, so this gives BE
Ian is the stock Scottish man's name; to play his part is to be Ian

explanation.surface: An abbreviated plea to take on a Scottish role in a play is rather ordinary.
explanation.definitionFit: Plebeian means belonging to the ordinary people, so lowly or common in taste.

clue.text: It's often clear who in Paris is wearing hat

indicators.note: the French word sits under the hat as a head wears a covering

parts.note: lid is slang for a hat
qui is French for who

explanation.surface: A person in Paris wearing a hat is often plain to see.
explanation.definitionFit: Water and many other fluids are transparent, so a fluid is often clear.

clue.text: Taking every tip to zip at the zip, I kip in a dip

indicators.note: every word's tip, its first letter, is taken in turn from the run of eight words

explanation.surface: A nonsense rhyme about zipping off to sleep in a hollow.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface is deliberate gibberish; 'in a dip' looks like part of the rhyme but 'a dip' is the definition, and 'in' supplies the final I.
explanation.definitionFit: Tzatziki is a Greek yoghurt-and-cucumber sauce served for scooping with bread, a classic dip.

clue.text: In every case, chart doors and base all out of place

indicators.note: every letter is displaced, so these words are rearranged

explanation.surface: Charts, doors and a base are all jumbled up and misplaced.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom means applying to everyone or everything without exception.

clue.text: Short sporting American and German making merry

indicators.note: short cuts the last letter from the word for an athlete

parts.note: jock is American slang for a sports-mad student
und is the German word for and

explanation.surface: A small American athlete and a German celebrate together.
explanation.definitionFit: Jocund is a literary adjective for cheerful and merry, in high spirits.

clue.text: What's repeated about sun god

parts.note: c, short for circa, means about
Horus is the falcon-headed Egyptian sky and sun god

explanation.surface: Someone asks what keeps being said about the sun god.
explanation.definitionFit: A refrain sung again after each verse of a song is the part repeated.

clue.text: Learned rude king elbows out queen

indicators.note: to elbow out is to push aside and take over, so one letter ousts another

parts.note: boorish means rude and ill-mannered
R, for Regina, is the abbreviation for queen
K is the chess abbreviation for king

explanation.surface: An educated but rude king shoves his queen aside.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Learned' reads as a verb in the surface but is the adjective (two syllables), studious.
explanation.definitionFit: A studious person fond of reading is scholarly, which is what learned means here.

clue.text: Old-fashioned butcher vied frantically with hen

indicators.note: acting frantically suggests wild disorder, so the letters are scrambled

explanation.surface: A butcher competes in a frenzy with a chicken.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom describes someone lagging behind current ideas or trends, hence dated.

clue.text: State where huntress's heart belongs

parts.note: in tells where something is
Diana is the Roman goddess of the hunt

explanation.surface: Asks where a huntress truly feels at home.
explanation.walkthrough: Read 'where huntress's heart belongs' as 'in Diana': the huntress's heart lies within the goddess herself.
explanation.definitionFit: Indiana is one of the fifty United States, in the Midwest.

clue.text: Gadgets communicate with it but old hotel gets confused

indicators.note: something confused is muddled, so these letters are mixed up

explanation.surface: Devices can talk to each other, but an elderly hotel manager is baffled.
explanation.definitionFit: This short-range wireless standard is what phones, earbuds and speakers use to link up.

clue.text: One providing backing with no force beneath

indicators.note: with no means lacking, so a letter is taken away

parts.note: a funder provides financial backing
F is the physics symbol for force

explanation.surface: A financial backer is left with no power below.
explanation.definitionFit: The two words are simple synonyms for lower than or below.

clue.text: Bit by bit while recalling tit, perhaps with grit, dull piece of s***

parts.note: in can mean during, while something is going on

indicators.note: recalling means calling back, so the word is read backwards

parts.note: a tit is one example of a bird
sand is fine grit
drab means dull and colourless
a piece of the starred word is its opening letter, the only one printed

explanation.surface: A rude rant about a small bird and grit, with a censored word.
explanation.walkthrough: 'recalling' turns BIRD into DRIB; the asterisked word gives only its first letter.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom means gradually, in small amounts at a time, little by little.

clue.text: Eastern town (and not that from which husband's gone missing)

parts.note: nor means and not

indicators.note: something gone missing is absent, so a letter is removed

parts.note: which can stand for that as a relative pronoun
H is the abbreviation for husband

explanation.surface: A town in the east, not the one a husband vanished from.
explanation.walkthrough: Norwich is a city in Norfolk, East Anglia, in England's east.
explanation.definitionFit: It is the county town of Norfolk in the east of England.

clue.text: Correct about what to wear

parts.note: re means about or concerning
a dress is something to wear

explanation.surface: A proper remark concerning choice of clothing.
explanation.definitionFit: To put right a wrong or imbalance is to rectify it, a synonym of correct.

clue.text: We're beaten — in fact I'm panicking

indicators.note: in shows the letters lie within the following words

explanation.surface: A defeated team admits that, truthfully, they are in a panic.
explanation.definitionFit: Kettledrums are struck with sticks, so the instruments speak of being beaten.

clue.text: As ruse might do, to be certain?

parts.note: to do something here is to make it, the action a ruse would perform

indicators.note: as means in the manner of a rearrangement here, the letters of ruse turned into a new word

explanation.surface: Asks whether a trick could be relied on for certainty.
explanation.walkthrough: A ruse, rearranged, makes 'sure': the whole clue describes what its own letters can do, so the question mark flags the play.
explanation.definitionFit: To check something so that one is confident of it is to ensure certainty.

clue.text: I printed blurrily in bold

indicators.note: a blurry print smears the letters, so they come out rearranged

explanation.surface: A printer confesses their text came out smudged in bold type.
explanation.definitionFit: A fearless, daring person is brave, which is what bold means.

clue.text: Sack with crack fixed room with morning snack?

parts.note: sack is slang for bed
and means with or plus
to crack is to break
fast means fixed firmly in place

explanation.surface: A bag with a mended split, then a room offering a light breakfast.
explanation.definitionFit: A guesthouse arrangement offers overnight lodging plus the first meal of the day.

clue.text: Tired round-the-world traveller Nellie given attention

indicators.note: the surname is given the word for attention inside it

parts.note: Nellie Bly was the American journalist who went round the world in 72 days in 1889
to give ear is to pay attention

explanation.surface: A famous globe-trotting journalist, worn out, is finally listened to.
explanation.definitionFit: Bleary eyes are dim and watery from fatigue, so weary and tired.

clue.text: Someone else proceeding with idea

parts.note: someone other than me is 'not I'
on means going ahead or continuing

explanation.surface: Another person goes ahead with a plan.
explanation.definitionFit: A notion is a belief or concept, a near synonym of an idea.

clue.text: A motley sounding group of tribes

indicators.note: sounding means as heard, so the phrase is spoken rather than spelt

parts.note: motley means patchy or variegated in colour

explanation.surface: A colourful, noisy band of tribespeople.
explanation.walkthrough: Said as 'a-patchy', the word matches the usual pronunciation of the tribal name.
explanation.definitionFit: These are several related Native American peoples of the Southwest, a group of tribes.

clue.text: Apply for release, with royal taking place of politician

indicators.note: taking the place of means one item substitutes for another

parts.note: to exempt is to release from an obligation
MP, Member of Parliament, is a politician
R is the abbreviation for royal, as in RN or RAF

explanation.surface: Seek to be freed, with a royal replacing a politician.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Apply' looks like 'apply for', but 'for' is a link; 'Apply' alone is the verb, as in apply pressure.
explanation.definitionFit: To exert force or pressure is to bring it to bear, to apply it.

clue.text: One vessel's ready for losing battle

parts.note: a means one
a mug is a drinking vessel, here possessive
game means willing or ready

explanation.surface: A single ship is prepared for a battle it will lose.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom describes a pointless activity that only a fool would pursue, one that cannot be won.

clue.text: Where does engineer go for dip? Answer!

parts.note: RE, the Royal Engineers, an army corps; possessive here
a pond is where one goes for a dip

explanation.surface: A quiz question: where does an engineer swim? Reply!
explanation.walkthrough: The Royal Engineers, RE, are a corps of the British Army; their swimming place would be the RE's pond.
explanation.definitionFit: To reply to a question is to give an answer, an imperative here.

clue.text: Clergyman always needs to tear about

indicators.note: about means around, so one word goes round another

parts.note: to rend is to tear
ever means always

explanation.surface: A cleric must constantly rush around.
explanation.walkthrough: 'tear about' wants to mean rush around, but 'about' is a container signal acting on 'tear'.
explanation.definitionFit: The title is the courtesy style of a member of the clergy, a minister or priest.
